title: Different dimensions of urbanization in East African cities and towns
abstract: Cities across the world are developing rapidly. Many studies have analysed this development in a one-dimensional way, mostly focussing on demographics or land cover. Yet, urbanization is in fact a multi-dimensional process, also characterized by economic transitions, changes in lifestyles, and increased connectivity. Consequently, the relationships between these dimensions remain unclear. This study presents the first systematic quantification of urban development in different dimensions for a large number of settlements. Specifically, we quantified urbanization in five dimensions for all settlements with over 10,000 inhabitants in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, using population, built-up land, and points-of-interest data on economic, social, and connectivity amenities. Our findings reveal medium to strong positive correlations (r = 0.54 to r = 0.76) between social, economic, and connectivity dimensions (all expressed per person), while others showed weak or no correlation. This suggests that different dimensions do not develop simultaneously, leading to varied urban profiles. Using K-means clustering, we identified six settlement types: a small cluster of metropoles, one type of medium-sized cities and four types of towns, which differ strongly in their physical, economic, social, and connectivity characteristics. These findings indicate that urban settlements develop in diverse ways with a high variation between the dimensions in smaller settlements. This highlights that threats and opportunities for sustainable urban development differ across settlements and require context-specific strategies while also drawing lessons from comparable settlements.

title: Introduction to Descent From Cherang'any Hills: Memoirs of a Reluctant Academic
source: Journal of Colonialism and Colonial History
abstract: Introduction to Descent From Cherang'any Hills: Memoirs of a Reluctant Academic Ryan Schappell Introduction Dr. B. E. Kipkorir's memoirs, Descent from Cherang'any Hills, provide an account of growing up in a Marakwet family and a society that was steadily changed by the tides of Colonialism and Christianity. The author writes from not only the distinct vantage of a village boy living in Kenya but also from one who received formal Western education at GAS Tambach, Alliance High School, Makerere University in Uganda, and then Cambridge University in England. In other words, although his memoirs could ignite the emotions of even a Stoic, he maintains academic discipline. While seeking a PhD at Cambridge University, Kipkorir married his first wife Lea, who had just obtained her master's degree from Harvard, in June 1969. The last chapter of Descent from Cherang'any Hills, "Till death do us part," primarily focuses on his early relationship and eventual marriage to her. The couple settled in Kenya soon after Kipkorir completed his PhD in December. They had four children together, all of which are grown today. Lea was eventually diagnosed with cancer which took her life in March 1999. Though the chapter discussing her is not included in the following extract, she is an important figure as she had pioneered early childhood education in Kenya. Kipkorir begins the book with his first memory at around age three (1942-1943) in the village of Ng'echer, where his father worked as an African Inland Mission (AIM) agent. Shortly thereafter, his mother abandoned his family, leaving his father to care for him and his four brothers. Kipkorir's family ultimately moved to Kapsowar which contained a large AIM settlement, naturally comprised of Christian adherents and families. While Kipkorir writes of his childhood, he also recounts the origins of AIM's work in Marakwet and their establishment of a mission station in Kapsowar. Simultaneously, he searches for an answer as to why one would convert from traditional African life to one prescribed by the newcomers, white men and women who touted a different set of cultural values and norms. In the section titled, "Concepts of God and Salvation," he compares beliefs from the "New Faith" with those of the Marakwet or Kalenjin tradition. He examines instances where missionaries could have made their religion more appealing to the Kalenjin, had they truly understood Kalenjin culture and language. After living five years in Kapsowar (1944-1948), he returned in 1950-1951, before permanently leaving and enrolling in boarding school. The final extract paints a vivid picture of Kipkorir's ethnic group, the Marakwet—which is actually a combination of six territorial clusters: Endo, Almo, Kiptani, Borkuut, Cherang'any, and Markweta; the name is, of course, a perversion from the latter group, a name originally given by Swahili traders and later adopted by the British. However, like many other ethnic groups in Kenya, the people now designated as the Marakwet had for centuries before the advent of British colonial administration settled along the western slopes of the Kerio Valley and adjoining Cherang'any Hills. These memories, such as those regarding his traditional grandfather, present village life on an intimate level, a level that could only have been written by a native. Kipkorir has worked as a Deputy Clerk of the Sirikwa County Council, lecturer at the University of Nairobi, Director of the Institute of African Studies, and Executive Chairman of the Kenya Commercial Bank; and has authored and published several other works. In another set of memoirs that he is expected to release, he is likely to discuss his career as Kenya's Ambassador to Washington as well as his remarriage and second family. What follows is a glimpse into Marakwet history—one altered by western ideology—told in the context of Kipkorir's life story. title: Religious institutions and the politics of access to basic services in displacement contexts:bureaucratising assistance or gifts of grace?
source: Research at the University of Copenhagen (University of Copenhagen)
abstract: This paper provides a study of religious institutions as service providers in contexts of crises and displacement. Religious institutions, as well as other non-state institutions, provide access to a vast range of resources and services (such as food, housing, clothes, counseling, money, and access to networks). In contexts of displacement access to basic services is formally regulated by one’s status (e.g. as refugee or national citizen) and by physical location (e.g. in settlements/camps or urban areas). The paper discusses what role religious institutions play when access to services provided by the state or the international humanitarian system is limited or non-existent and what kind of relations of exchange that is at stake. Empirically the project deals with Congolese churches in Kampala, Uganda of which many pastors and members have refugee status. The paper analyses the range and categories of services provided by churches and the categorization of people gaining access to these resources. The furthermore paper discusses what forms of recognition engaging in these more material relations of exchange entail, as well as the forms of authority that are established.

title: Defiance through many means: The urbanities of African universities. A commentary on Patricia Daley and Amber Murrey's ‘Defiant scholarship: Dismantling coloniality in contemporary African geographies’.
abstract: Daley and Murrey (2022) in this critical intervention, reiterate the importance of African intellectual production as not only a long occluded register and a long-standing missed opportunity, but as acts of defiance. While certain radical political economy threads of African scholarship could in some quarters be seen as crowding out a more heterogenous actual canon, defiance here is not only in response to the positionality of African thought in a global arena but also in terms of what constitutes legitimate institutions and practices of knowledge formation and conveyance. For African universities, which for long periods of time enjoined the self-defeating game of trying to prove themselves better than their European counterparts as the criteria for being taken seriously, which was largely never forthcoming, the subsequent spiraling down of motivation or, more commonly, contentment with just the capacity to get by rendered universities largely irrelevant to the elaboration of ‘real economies’ and social innovation on the ground. Still, the inordinate efforts of many African academics who kept a sharp eye on all kinds of social and political processes underway, who never left for the greener pastures of Western academia, and who produced prolific bodies of work with their students remain a testament to the vision of African academia as a vanguard for social transformation. Particularly important are all of those archivists that painstakingly collected and maintained different kinds of writing, as well as audio-visual productions, many of which were never published or distributed, at least formally. These are witnesses to the often wild, unruly and intensely rhizomatic character of African reflexivity, indifferent to the conventions of empirical legitimation or normative academic niceties. A critical question would seem to what extent African universities might exemplify an epistemological disobedience in its very institutional foundations, while still appearing as universities and their concomitant function as conveyors of knowledge and guarantors of particular knowledge practices. Where might the university go, and what might it become? These are difficult conditions given the inordinate effort expended in simply trying to manage minimal levels of functioning, i.e. libraries that enable access to current publications, classrooms equipped with basic audio-visual capacities let alone smart technologies, or the consistency of academic schedules ridden frequently by labour disputes and politically-motivated closures. While defiant scholarship ‘attends to the ways in which coloniality effects forms of distortion, denial, negation, rejection and assassination of decolonial world senses and anti-imperial and anti-racist knowledges and projects for epistemic justice’ (Daley & Murrey, 2022: 168) it also valorizes the albeit often ragged, tremulous attempts to stand aside, to risk all kinds of distortions in efforts to shift the terms of the hegemonic academic game. This is what many African universities ended up doing, at least by default. From the late 1970's to the early 1990's Fourah Bay University in Freetown was at the center of militant challenges to the prevailing political order and a context for intense contestation among different visions and points of view, and importantly, where the distinctions between students and non-students, and class backgrounds often fell away in practices that upended any semblance of normative teaching but that continuously experimented with the boundaries of pedagogy, which for some included revolutionary practice. In Khartoum during the 1980's, university classrooms were punctuated by constant jockeying for position among different political tendencies. While departments, dormitories and cafeterias were too frequently balkanized according to specific affiliations, at least there was sufficient co-presence among the student body so that divergent ideas would still have an impact on each other. At the university's theater school, which has an implicit affirmative action policy to include Communists, Baathists, Islamicists, Ansar and Christians from all regions of Sudan, intensive fights in the hostels were converted into conjointly run community theater projects aimed at sensing the ‘real’ political orientations of different neighbourhoods across the city. During several years of the protracted civil war in Cote d'Ivoire, the university, Félix Houphouët-Boigny, became the bastion of youthful militants, the Young Patriots, supporting Laurent Gbagbo, who problematically turned the university into a kind of mafia organization aimed at enabling the seizure of wealth from an older generation and its redistribution across the low income districts of Adjame Texas, Port Bouet, and Yopougon. The University of Kinshasa for years has functioned as one of the city's largest informal settlements, where if formal teaching has largely ceased, then scores of autonomous collectives intent upon learning proliferate. None of these stories embody a clear-cut ethically or politically progressive agenda. They are not defiant in terms of the content of curriculum or pedagogical practice. But they do indicate the various ways in which universities have become instantiated in the complicated landscapes of African urban and national politics. While universities such as Makerere are held up as exemplary instances of the ways in which academic departments and researchers are inserted across Uganda as technical advisors to rural collectives, designers of innovative sanitation systems for small towns, training parents as daycare personnel in low income settlements, to designing policy frameworks for local government finance, many African universities have found themselves maintaining porous boundaries, enfolding all kinds of legitimate and nefarious activities. Organizations like the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa, although heavily dependent upon foreign funding, have for decades attempted to pursue not only a Pan-African ethos in terms of curricula and publication, but also in practice, forging multiple opportunities for scholars from different African nations to work closely with each other on common projects; to always experiment with the terms of what it meant to be African. While many of the key intellectuals Daley and Murrey cite were important members of CODESRIA, it was all of the convocations among young scholars, through national and regional working groups, summer schools and publication projects that continuously worked to circumvent linguistic, ethnic and disciplinary divides to both do what was needed to attain academic credibility and foster forms of collaboration and support that would be mobilized over the years to aid a broad range of individual cultural and political projects. Here, import was ceded to the formation of cohorts, of ongoing relationships that could be called upon to support a wide range of challenges to individual universities, multilateral donors and political bodies. While organizations like CODESRIA usually shied away from discussions of blackness within the regional context, preferring to amplify a pan African identity that was united in struggles against imperialism and enduring coloniality, many universities were nevertheless sites of the kinds of intersecting discourses on racialism and black geographies that the authors point to. Far from dismissing the relevance of blackness in African contexts, it was often invoked in the sense of marking particular kinds of distinctions of eligibility, cultural practice, entitlement and social capacity within student bodies, with the proliferation of different vernaculars which may not have explicitly invoked ‘blackness’, but ended up doing ‘its’ work anyway. At the University of Khartoum, for example, blackness both connoted degrees of legitimacy, inexplicable wisdom, denigration, ineligibility and spiritual attainment, all across different, oscillating registers of use and according to different genealogies of the people being referred to. This was coupled to intricate and shifting hierarchies as to who owed deference to whom. In Abidjan, in the frequent pitched battles between university students from (Christian) Port Bouet and neighbouring (Muslim) Koumassi, battle cries incorporated frequent reference to American racial terms of derogation. On the other hand, for some university students at Chiekh Anta Diop in Dakar or at the University of Douala, blackness was an ‘open field’, something to be engaged and appropriated for the realm of extraordinary endeavors. Perhaps refused at the level of self-attribution, it was nevertheless folded into everyday vernaculars as almost cosmological field of play and striving, a universe of considerations that were beyond the structuring of any political regime or historical moment, and thus generative beyond the available measures of efficacy and judgment. For university students who often needed to fail in order to keep a roof over their heads and ensure two meals a day, for students who worked hard to complete curricula they knew was woefully outdated, for students who always felt behind the rest of the world, blackness was something beyond all of that. Not a limiting condition; not a marker of ontological singularity, but rather as something extraterrestrial, defiant of any terms the earth might offer to ascribe value to their lives.

title: Women's association raises a community from a slum.
abstract: The impact of post-British colonialism in Jinja, Uganda, is examined, with particular emphasis being given to the involvement of the Masese Women's Association in revival efforts in Jinja, Uganda has gone through periods of political upheaval resulting from civil strife during Idi Amin's rule in 1971-78. Refugees had started to squat in the "Masese" slum area and were experiencing destitute poverty and unemployment. In response to such conditions, citizens, governments, and nongovernmental organizations, in association with the Masese Women's Association, engaged in an effort called the Masese Women's Self Help Projects with the aim of bringing about a change in the way of life for the people in Jinja, Uganda. A Housing and Human Settlement Upgrading Program was created to establish a settlement and credit plan that would enable women to acquire secure land tenure and production materials for housing. The project also developed a community infrastructure for employment, health, and education services. The women's organization encountered many obstacles in the realization of these housing and settlement projects, among them illiteracy and traditional thinking and practices of the kind that have confined Ugandan women to the private sphere.

title: GIS AND MULTI-CRITERIA BASED ANALYSIS FOR BEST SOLID WASTE DISPOSAL SITE SELECTION INSHASHAMENE TOWN, ETHIOPIA
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: For this work first best experiences of solid waste management and site selection planning of Grahams town , South Africa and Kampala city of Uganda countries, suitable sites were studied. Multi criteria GIS based technique was used to identify suitable sites for waste disposal. The data used for applying multi criteria GIS based site selection are city base map, topography, settlements (urban center distance), roads network map, proposed railways route, slope, land use map, abattoir site, streams, important buildings, prevailing wind directions, residence land use, social service distribution map, greenery and sensitive area, floodplains, high tension line, cemetery area, utility map of the city, potential expansion area and master plan document and photo were used. In addition structural plan and city greenery and beautification reports (2013), city capital investment plan report (2012/13), city observation and manuals on Ethiopian urban planning and implementation and environmental protection authority guidelines (2002, 2003, and 2007) and individual knowledge on the site were used to set selection criteria. The results obtained provide most suitable areas for landfill sites in the study area.

title: Beyond Borders: The New Architecture of Transitional Justice?
abstract: The assertion by a national of the former Yugoslavia that a regional approach to transitional justice was needed ‘because we were killing each other regionally’1 appears self-evident and uncontroversial at one level. However, the implications are highly controversial for the simple reason that transitional justice was initially conceived within a national framework. That said, the disintegration of certain states, the reconstitution of national identities, the emergence of transnational nonstate actors such as the ‘Islamic State’ or Boko Haram and the intervention of the international criminal justice system in numerous conflicts have called on us to challenge the immutability of the nation state as a primary means of reflecting on and organizing transitional justice approaches. The nation state, once the alpha and omega of international relations and the cornerstone of transitional justice, is being challenged on multiple fronts: from neoliberal globalization, which accelerates the free movement of people and capital, thereby undermining governments’ capacity to act; to the development of information technologies that create new communities indifferent to national spaces; and the power of multinationals, which generate higher revenue than the gross domestic product of some countries. In the Middle East, the so-called Islamic State defied the Syrian–Iraqi border to enforce its ‘caliphate’2 while also radicalizing young Europeans through internet propaganda. At the same time, in the comfort of an air-conditioned office near Las Vegas, armed solely with joysticks, US military drone pilots inflict death 7,500 miles away, a reality that remains only virtual to them. In Europe and Africa, micro nationalisms have asserted themselves, rocking the very core of state legitimacy. An extreme example is Libya, where three governments claim to govern, sending shock waves of destabilization across the Sahel region. Elsewhere, such as in the Central African Republic (CAR) and Mali, governments have lost control of significant sections of their territory. At the same time, the dramatic rise of nationalism and populism, often accompanied by rising xenophobia and widespread withdrawal into narrowly circumscribed identity politics, is gaining ground in Europe and the US. These developments are evident in the building of new walls against migrants and refugees, and the retreat of multilateral diplomacy. When transitional justice mechanisms were developed and theorized at the end of the 1980s and in the following decade, they focused primarily on the (re)birth of fragile democracies, empowered by negotiated settlements with authoritarian regimes, towards acknowledging human rights violations committed by the previous regime while institutionalizing the rule of law within a clearly defined national space. This was the experience of Argentina and Chile transitioning from military dictatorships, of the former communist regimes in Central and Eastern Europe, and of South Africa, countries with strong institutions in which transitional justice symbolically embodied democratic change. The optimism of the immediate post-Cold War fuelled a teleological vision of societies’ moral progress revolving around the project of liberal democracy, in a world dominated by an American superpower. This vision of the march of history constitutes transitional justice’s DNA, a vision that is now being contested, as demonstrated by the focus of this Special Issue. The paradigm of transitional justice, which was expected to lead people gradually towards democratic renewal embodied by the development of the rule of law and international justice, has been increasingly challenged. The expected dividends of peace are long gone and arms sales3 are skyrocketing, as are the number of refugees.4 A progressive adherence to the International Criminal Court (ICC) has given way to a number of withdrawals from the Court, while Syria has been a bloody battlefield for more than five years, forcing more than half of its population of 22 million to flee their homes. This Special Issue reflects on the implications of this changing context for the very core of transitional justice. Processes of change no longer fall easily within a model that focuses on a transition from an oppressive to a democratic regime. Instead, they increasingly signify the redistribution of national spaces and the remodelling of identities caught up in the highly complex transition from war to peace. Transitional justice faces these questions alongside other complex challenges regarding its relevance to new peacebuilding demands and concerns about its legitimacy and its impact on victims. The CAR is in many respects a tragic laboratory in which a new architecture of transitional justice is being formulated. Interventions are taking place at different levels, ranging from heads of districts and traditional leaders to the ICC, and including the implementation of a truth commission and a hybrid special criminal court. The hope is that these levels of intervention will somehow provide a holistic solution and fertilize one another. The challenges are considerable given that most of the country remains in the hands of armed groups, some of which are pressing for secession. In those extreme conditions, what mechanisms can best coordinate the different levels of action, stretching from a remote village in northern CAR to The Hague? And what links need to be established between those justice mechanisms and questions of governance, security and disarmament? These are formidable challenges that must be met to achieve the aims of peace and reconstruction. Transitional justice is therefore being plunged into an environment that is experiencing ongoing turmoil. In a context in which borders – identity, political and judicial – are constantly being redefined, there is a need to examine some of the new challenges facing transitional justice, especially those dealing with the dynamics of some African state parties’ rejection of and withdrawal from the ICC. This is the first point on which various of the Special Issue authors reflect, with each tackling a specific aspect of this challenge. Geoffrey Lugano analyzes the victorious strategy, constructed through regional solidarity and a subtle combination of cooperation and noncooperation with the ICC, led by ICC accused Uhuru Kenyatta and William Ruto in Kenya. Through the arrest of another ICC accused, Dominic Ongwen of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA), Adam Branch meticulously deciphers how the ICC found itself plunged into this brutal geopolitical reality. Franziska Boehme examines the process and motivations that drove South Africa’s withdrawal from the ICC, whereas Matiangai Sirleaf addresses the central question of justice legitimacy by analyzing the Malabo Protocol, which anticipates the creation of the first permanent regional criminal court under the guidance of the African Union (AU). The second point addressed by authors in this issue focuses on border negotiations that draw on, or are grounded in, transitional justice mechanisms in countries that were not independent 30 years ago (the Ukraine and the republics of the former Yugoslavia), whose territory has drastically evolved (the unification of the two Germanys) or whose status is still unsettled (Taiwan). Ian and Jamie Rowen decipher the political and identity-framing objectives of the new truth commission in Taiwan, while Anja Mihr analyzes the process through which transitional justice mechanisms are just as likely to consolidate democratic regimes as autocracies. Ilya Nuzov examines how, in the former Soviet space, memory policies that were designed to secure fragile identities led to opposite outcomes, creating ideological conditions conducive to both the annexation of Crimea by Russia and the Donbas conflict. Meanwhile, Denisa Kostovicova reminds us that the worst is not always certain: through a quantitative and qualitative analysis, she demonstrates how former Yugoslavia’s civil societies laid the foundation for a narrative that was simultaneously regional, plural and inclusive of war crimes committed in the Balkans during the 1990s. The judicial process that led to former Chadian president Hissène Habré’s trial 25 years after having been overthrown is revealing of the new architecture of transitional justice. This ‘interminable legal and political soap opera,’5 as coined by Desmond Tutu, embodies the way in which transitional justice adapts and is reshaped at the interface of these hybrid and cross-fertilization processes, detached from the smooth and pure image of a well-oiled judicial machine. Plunged into the reality of power relations, a multiplicity of actors confronted one another at local, regional and international levels. This ultimately resulted in the AU and Senegal creating the first ad hoc criminal court, the Extraordinary African Chambers. In 2016 in Dakar, thousands of kilometres away from Chad, they judged the former president for crimes he had committed in his own country. Souleymane Guengueng was one of the figureheads in the fight to secure Habré’s prosecution. Tortured to the verge of blindness, he was one of the few survivors of the dictator’s notorious death cells. He swore an oath that, should he come out alive, he would use his energy to have the former dictator convicted. With other victims, Guengueng embodied this fight. He described himself as ‘a little bird in the branches,’ but, as he said proudly, he became ‘larger than Hissène Habré had ever been’ because justice was done.6 This image of a little bird in the branches evokes vulnerability and local roots. The determination and courage of Habré’s victims, consolidated through local associations in N’Djamena, were supported by Chadian human rights nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), as well as international human rights organizations, which offered support and expertise as well as assistance in securing funds. The prosecution also involved the willingness of Belgium’s justice architecture to prosecute the former dictator in accordance with the principle of universal jurisdiction, followed by the intervention of the UN Committee against Torture, which repeated requests for the prosecution of Habré, and, finally, the ICC’s judgment, which was consistent with this line.7 It took presidential elections in Senegal to finally break the political stranglehold preventing the trial, as well as the promise of Chadian and western funding for the AU and Senegal to finally decide to create the Extraordinary African Chambers under Senegalese jurisdiction. The Habré case demonstrates how, under the initial pressure of local victims’ associations, a case essentially internal8 to Chad was regionalized and internationalized to finally be judged in an ad hoc tribunal of a third country more than 3,000 kilometres from the concerned society, and including the legitimacy of the AU. In many respects, therefore, it is a paradigm for transitional justice’s new architecture. It demonstrates the primacy of civil society, the role of the international media, the need for international NGOs’ judicial expertise,9 the respective weight of states – Belgium and Senegal – and of the UN, as well as the legitimacy granted by a regional institution, the AU. Ultimately, therefore, the exercise of justice does not appear to be the product of a decontextualized institution but rather the final episode of a power struggle, a 15-year legal and political fight that unfolded on three continents, in N’Djamena, Dakar, Addis Ababa, New York, Brussels, Geneva and The Hague. The fight won by Guengueng and his fellow former captives is precisely the one that the ICC lost, at least temporarily: the fight for legitimacy. The ICC could neither represent victims nor widely embody the struggle against impunity. The Court aroused tremendous hope for civil societies in Africa, but was never able to capitalize on this original sympathy. In its defence, the ICC was not designed to undertake historical trials such as the Habré case. The justice it dispenses engages the present and the future. The belligerents among the defendants are part of multiple military and political fights and the judicial field is now one of their battlefields – a field in which their destiny and their reason for being is at play. For them, international justice is a zero-sum game in which the loser is criminalized and can see their country isolated, treated like a pariah, or even become the object of boycotts or sanctions. In the middle of the 19th century, the German writer and politician Ludwig von Rochau invented the term ‘Realpolitik’ to describe a telescoping of the aspirations for progress represented by the Age of Enlightenment and the power games between nascent nation states. A century and half later, we can talk about Realjustice to describe a new reality in which human rights discourse, the development of international justice and interstate power struggles jostle for primacy. Realjustice reflects states’ determination to legitimate their political and moral version of history while preserving their own interests in a conflict or a crisis. When conducted successfully, Realjustice provides political legitimacy, enabling states to impose their version of events in the public space by distributing roles between victims and war criminals using the discourse of international humanitarian law. Many African governments have used this judicial weapon to their own benefit. Taking advantage of their public’s thirst for justice and the seduction of a fight against impunity, they invited the ICC in in order to criminalize their opponents and enemies while avoiding any sanctions themselves. This is what occurred in Uganda, where the ICC charged LRA leaders, whereas the crimes presumably committed by the Ugandan army were never subjected to judicial proceedings from the ICC. This unilateral justice was also demonstrated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Apart from warlords, the ICC charged Jean-Pierre Bemba, President Joseph Kabila’s main opponent, while the elections were looming. Likewise, in Côte d’Ivoire, the ICC addressed only one side of the coin, the defeated former president, Laurent Gbagbo.10 It was solely when the Court sought to emancipate and deal with heads of state – the Sudanese president, Omar al-Bashir – that the AU distanced itself from the ICC. Since the actions of international justice were regarded as hostile to their interests, African governments elaborated three strategies: the immediate and absolute refusal to cooperate with the ICC; interference by inflating competing ‘judicial truths’; and, finally, a subtle mix of cooperation and noncooperation with the Court, backed by regional solidarity. Directly defying the Court has proven a difficult path for some countries. During its first term, the George W. Bush administration initiated this ICC rejection strategy. It sought to guarantee US citizens’ immunity from the Court and to thwart other states from acceding to the Rome Statute without taking US concerns into account. It penalized more than 20 countries for supporting the ICC. Despite its leverage, the Bush administration lost this judicial and political battle. Charged in 2009 by the ICC, al-Bashir refused to cooperate with the Court. He was able to get the AU to call on its members not to collaborate with the ICC, but this empty-chair policy presents significant risks for it sows the seeds of a narrative of international justice within the international public space. More efficient than the empty-chair policy, some governments used the technique of interference by inflating competing ‘judicial truths.’ The paradigmatic example of this is the Turkish–Israeli confrontation following the boarding and inspection of the flotilla heading to Gaza in 2010, an action that provoked the death of 10 Turkish citizens. Drawing lessons from the political failure of its boycott of the Goldstone Commission, the Israeli government played the card of one-upmanship of reports. title: Advancing Global Health Education Through Structured Engagement: The S.E.R.V.E Program
source: Journal of acute care and resuscitation.
abstract: Introduction Volunteering is defined as intentional, non-obligatory behavior aimed at societal benefit without expectation of material reward.[1] It is increasingly recognized as a significant component of undergraduate extracurricular medical education with potential academic, psychological, and professional benefits. Studies indicate that volunteerism is increasingly common among undergraduates, with a significant proportion of medical students engaging in volunteer activities, often within their university settings.[2] Such volunteer activities range from direct patient care and public health initiatives to administrative support and crisis response. These engagements are driven by diverse motivations, including skill acquisition, career enhancement, academic reinforcement, and altruistic contributions to society. Notably, volunteering has been shown to positively influence medical students’ psychological well-being and personal development, mitigating the stressors and burnout levels inherent in medical training.[3,4] Furthermore, participation in community service projects fosters leadership skills, teaches valuable lessons, and heightens awareness of community health needs, while simultaneously enhancing essential soft skills such as communication, empathy, and decision-making. Volunteering has also demonstrated. A positive association with academic performance, as evidenced by improved grade point averages and residency outcomes. Empirical evidence suggests a positive correlation between volunteering and academic performance, potentially through the augmentation of intrinsic motivation.[1] Medical school admission committees, recognizing the importance of humanistic qualities alongside academic prowess, are increasingly emphasizing community service as a marker of potential for compassionate care.[5] Service-learning is an educational approach that integrates community service with structured academic learning and reflective activities. In response, medical schools are integrating service-learning opportunities into their curricula, aiming to cultivate altruistic tendencies and provide students with practical, real-world experiences. These initiatives range from structured, curriculum-based service-learning to voluntary community service, each contributing uniquely to students’ professional development.[5] Interprofessional education (IPE) has gained prominence in healthcare training, promoting collaborative learning among students from different healthcare disciplines. The World Health Organization defines IPE as an educational model in which “two or more professions learn about, from, and with each other to enable effective collaboration and improve health outcomes.”[6] Clinical shadowing, a component of IPE, allows students to observe the roles of various healthcare professionals, enhancing their understanding of team-based care, interprofessional communication, and ethical considerations in patient management.[7] IPE and clinical shadowing are also emerging as vital components, fostering collaborative practice competencies and broadening students’ perspectives on patient care.[6-8] Ultimately, integrating volunteering, IPE, and international clinical experience into medical curricula aims to cultivate well-rounded physicians capable of addressing the complex healthcare needs of diverse populations. Moreover, international medical placements, particularly in resource-limited settings like East and Central Africa offer unique opportunities for students to gain exposure to diverse healthcare systems, enhance clinical skills, and develop global healthcare awareness. These experiences not only broaden students’ clinical knowledge by exposing them to a wider range of diseases and treatment modalities but also foster personal growth and cultural competency. Participating in clinical rotations in low-resource environments has been shown to cultivate adaptability, resilience, and cross-cultural competence among students, thereby reinforcing their ability to provide equitable care in diverse settings.[8] Additionally, these experiences contribute to professional networking, knowledge exchange, and future engagement in global health initiatives. International medical placements also serve as transformative experiences for medical students, offering exposure to diverse healthcare systems, resource-limited settings, and global health challenges. Given the significant academic, professional, and personal benefits associated with volunteering, structured community service programs should be considered a fundamental component of medical education. The integration of volunteerism, service-learning, and interprofessional collaboration within medical training not only enhances students’ competencies but also fosters a commitment to lifelong learning, humanistic care, and societal responsibility. The S.E.R.V.E Program The S.E.R.V.E (Shadowing, Engaging, Reaching-Out, Volunteering, Educating) program, created by HumanResus International Organization, is a transformative initiative aimed at advancing global health education and engagement. As a non-governmental organization registered in Sudan and Uganda, HumanResus has crafted this program to offer international students and early-career physicians structured opportunities for clinical exposure, community service, volunteering, and professional development in resource-limited settings. By integrating volunteering, shadowing, and outreach experiences with academic objectives, the S.E.R.V.E program fosters a commitment to global health equity while empowering participants to address healthcare disparities meaningfully. This multi-faceted approach transcends the limitations of isolated experiences, empowering clinical acumen while enhancing profound appreciation for the social determinants of health. Through strategic collaborations with reputable organizations such as the Association of Ambulance Professionals of Uganda (AAPU), the Resuscitation Council of the College of Anesthesiologists and Intensivists of Sri Lanka, and the World Congress of Trauma and Emergency Leagues in Brazil, the program provides participants with direct engagement in healthcare systems around the world. This international framework allows for firsthand insights into medical practices, emergency response, and community-driven health initiatives. At the core of the program is a structured, experiential learning model designed to enhance medical education and professional competence. This model encompasses hospital-based clinical shadowing, pre-hospital and ambulance-based emergency medical training, community outreach, and focused educational sessions, ensuring a well-rounded, multidisciplinary learning experience. By cultivating skills and knowledge pertinent to global health challenges, the program also emphasizes the development of cultural competency, ethical medical practice, and a sustained commitment to service. Ultimately, S.E.R.V.E program contributes to the fortification of global healthcare systems by cultivating a cohort of socially responsible and globally aware healthcare professionals. Bridging Clinical Education and Community Service The multi-faceted approach at the core of this program seamlessly integrates clinical immersion with community engagement, providing participants with a comprehensive understanding of healthcare in diverse contexts. Participants engage in clinical shadowing at a full-time medical institution, allowing them to gain firsthand exposure to acute care across multiple medical disciplines. This intensive experience is further enriched by shadowing first responders in ambulance teams, thereby offering vital insights into pre-hospital emergency care, an essential yet often underrepresented aspect of medical education. The clinical exposure is complemented by engagement in primary care services within challenged and displaced communities, including refugee populations. This integration of clinical experience with humanitarian aid is pivotal in addressing health disparities in these vulnerable settings. Beyond the clinical environment, the program extends its initiatives to humanitarian efforts in refugee settlements. Participants not only provide direct clinical services but also assist in screening for prevalent health issues faced by these communities, such as depression and anxiety disorders, chronic medical conditions, and common skeletal and joint disorders. Additionally, they facilitate necessary physical therapy support and community training in first aid, basic emergency procedures, and life support techniques. Moreover, participants contribute to essential daily support services, including meal provision, hygiene promotion, and psychosocial assistance for displaced populations. This comprehensive integration of clinical and community-based experiences equips participants with a holistic perspective on healthcare, one that transcends traditional clinical interventions and acknowledges the significant socio-economic and psychological determinants of health. Through this program, participants are not only trained as clinicians but also as advocates for health equity, reinforcing the importance of addressing the broader determinants of health in their future medical careers. Training and Preparing, Getting Ready to Serve Community-based interventions play a vital role in preparing volunteers operating in diverse and unpredictable environments. The necessity for robust training, particularly in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), psychological and medical first aid training, is essential for equipping volunteers to provide life-saving interventions during emergencies [Figure 1]. Evidence supports the efficacy of targeted basic life support (BLS) training in bolstering community resilience. By the Regional Crisis Center Team on CPR and Automated External Defibrillator utilization, the teams showed enhanced local preparedness for cardiac emergencies.[9]Figure 1: First aid training for Sudanese refugees by S.E.R.V.E program student volunteersA distinctive feature of the S.E.R.V.E program is its structured educational framework. Participants receive training and certification in BLS, First Aid, Bleeding Control, and a specialized S.E.R.V.E curriculum covering essential competencies such as safety, communication, empathy, and professionalism [Figure 1]. This evidence-based training model not only enhances participants’ practical skills but also reinforces the ethical and humanistic aspects of medical practice. Furthermore, the program’s emphasis on emergency medical care training aligns with global efforts to strengthen healthcare systems in low-resource settings. By equipping participants with resuscitation skills and acute care competencies, the initiative contributes to building a workforce capable of responding to medical emergencies both within and beyond Uganda. In summary, integrating CPR and BLS training into community volunteer programs is crucial for enhancing preparedness and health outcomes among vulnerable populations. Community-based interventions are crucial for preparing volunteers in diverse and unpredictable environments. Robust training protocols, particularly in necessary out-of-hospital emergency skills, are essential for equipping volunteers to provide basic life-saving interventions during emergencies. Training Vulnerable Communities to Face Their Health Challenges Evidence indicates that BLS education for refugee populations is both feasible and effective in increasing their willingness to perform CPR, thus improving survival rates following cardiac arrest [Figure 2].[10] Notably, certain demographic characteristics, such as age and educational level, may indicate certain groups that would benefit from advanced life support training.[10] Additionally, fostering community collaboration is essential in addressing mental health disparities among immigrant populations. Training programs like mental health first aid effectively equip advocates in immigrant communities to provide culturally sensitive support.[11]Figure 2: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation training for Sudanese refugees by S.E.R.V.E program student volunteersHowever, challenges such as significant health literacy barriers hinder vulnerable populations, including refugees, making it difficult for them to comprehend health information and navigate emergencies.[12] Addressing language barriers and improving access to resources and navigation skills within health systems are vital. Addressing health literacy challenges and promoting community collaboration are integral components of improving health outcomes among vulnerable populations. Addressing Mental Health Needs among Refugee Populations The relevance of the S.E.R.V.E program extends beyond traditional medical training, as evidenced by its engagement with refugee communities. The recent cross-sectional study conducted by a S.E.R.V.E Program batch in the Kiryandongo Refugee Settlement underscores the pressing mental health challenges faced by Sudanese refugees, with findings indicating a 43% prevalence of moderate to severe depression and a 24% prevalence of moderate to severe anxiety. These statistics highlight the urgent need for targeted mental health interventions that are culturally sensitive and gender-responsive.[13] Given the program’s active involvement in refugee support, it has the potential to serve as a platform for implementing mental health initiatives. Standardized screenings, psychological first aid training, and trauma-informed care approaches that could be integrated into the program’s existing structure, ensuring that participants are equipped to address both the physical and psychological health needs of vulnerable populations. A Model for Sustainable Global Health Collaboration The formalized partnership between HumanResus International and AAPU, as outlined in their Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), exemplifies a sustainable model for global health collaboration. By delineating clear roles, HumanResus overseeing application processes, logistics, and participant coordination, while AAPU facilitates clinical placements and training, the agreement ensures the program’s operational efficiency and long-term sustainability. Importantly, while the MOU does not establish legal or financial obligations between the parties, it represents a strategic commitment to fostering meaningful cooperation in healthcare education. This collaborative framework could serve as a blueprint for similar initiatives worldwide, demonstrating the value of interdisciplinary partnerships in advancing medical training and humanitarian service. Conclusion The S.E.R.V.E program stands as a testament to the transformative potential of structured global health education. By integrating clinical exposure, community service, and targeted training, the initiative not only enhances participants’ professional development but also contributes to healthcare capacity-building in underserved regions [Figure 3]. Moreover, its engagement with refugee populations highlights the intersection between medical education and humanitarian response, reinforcing the need for holistic, inclusive approaches to global health challenges.Figure 3: S.E.R.V.E program, another successful day of student volunteering and refugee serviceAs the program continues to evolve, expanding its scope to include mental health interventions, a broader public health initiatives could further amplify its impact. In an era where healthcare inequities persist, initiatives like S.E.R.V.E exemplify the role of structured, collaborative programs in preparing future healthcare professionals to navigate the complexities of global health with competence, compassion, and cultural awareness. title: Giraffe and okapi: Africa's forgotten megafauna
abstract: The Giraffidae family includes only two living species of ungulates: the giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis) and the okapi (Okapia johnstoni), both restricted to the African continent. Taxonomically, the Giraffa and Okapia genera separated from each other approximately 16 million years ago (Hassanin et al., 2012), and they now exhibit as many differences as similarities. Today Okapia is represented by one species (Okapia johnstoni; Hart, 2013), though with surprisingly high genetic variation (Stanton et al., 2014), whereas nine subspecies of giraffe are currently recognized (although ongoing research is underway): Giraffa camelopardalis angolensis, G. c. antiquorum, G. c. camelopardalis, G. c. giraffa, G. c. peralta, G. c. reticulata, G. c. rothschildi, G. c. thornicrofti and G. c. tippelskirchi; Giraffe Conservation Foundation, 2013; Bock et al., 2014). At first sight, these two species look quite different, but they share a number of common features, including elongated necks and long, dark-coloured tongues (both adaptations for feeding on tree leaves), lobed canine teeth and skin-covered horns called ossicones (Bodmer & Rabb, 1992). With their unique coat pattern – squares for giraffe and stripes for okapi – both species are also individually identifiable, a very useful characteristic in ecological studies (see Halloran, Murdoch & Becker, 2015; for an example). While okapi are restricted to the dense, lowland rainforests of central and north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC; although there have been historic and current reports of okapi in western Uganda, e.g. Kingdon, 1979), giraffe historically roamed the open savannahs encircling this region, across much of the rest of Africa. Giraffe now occur patchily in 21 countries, from Niger to Central and East Africa and down to southern Africa (Giraffe Conservation Foundation, 2013). Large herbivores, such as giraffe and okapi, play a central role in ecosystems, standing between plants and predators (Danell et al., 2006). Both species are vulnerable to predators, especially leopards for the okapi (Hart & Hart, 1988b) and lions for the giraffe (Hayward & Kerley, 2005). Like other large African ungulates, the giraffe is an agent of change in habitats and landscapes. It opens up areas and stimulates the growth of browsing forage for other species (Giraffe Conservation Foundation, 2013). The okapi is unique among the large mammals of the Ituri forest in having a diet composed solely of understory foliage (Hart & Hart, 1988a). Their role in the functioning of African ecosystems is one key reason to conserve giraffid populations in the wild, although dedicated studies are still needed for okapi. While the giraffe can boast more global fame, both giraffid species are internationally popular in zoos and are also emblematic of the ecosystems and countries in which they live. The giraffe is the national animal of Tanzania and may not be hunted in countries such as Botswana, Niger and Zambia as it is considered to be ‘royal’ (Giraffe Conservation Foundation, 2013). The okapi is a source of national pride for DRC, appearing on the banknotes of the Congolese franc and the logo of the national conservation agency, and has a World Heritage Site named after it, the Okapi Wildlife Reserve. Despite their iconic status, the giraffe and the okapi are relatively poorly studied and there is a general lack of knowledge on the key factors affecting their demographic rates. Until recently, neither species was considered threatened and relatively few studies had been conducted on their population dynamics and ecology (Quinn, Queslin & Kümpel, 2013; Bercovitch & Deacon, 2015). However, recent surveys and reviews have highlighted notable reductions in their geographical ranges and declines in their populations (Giraffe Conservation Foundation, 2013; Kümpel, Quinn & Grange, 2015). According to the Giraffe Conservation Foundation (2013), the number of giraffe in Africa has decreased by >43% since 1998, with less than 80,000 giraffes remaining today. Similarly, the okapi has probably experienced a 50% population decline over the last two decades (Kümpel, Quinn & Grange, 2015; Mallon et al., 2013). The main threats facing both giraffid species, to varying extents across their ranges, include habitat loss and degradation, human encroachment and settlement, poaching, war and civil unrest (Giraffe Conservation Foundation, 2013; Hart, 2013; Quinn et al., in press). Subpopulations of both species are becoming increasingly fragmented. In 2013, an IUCN Red List reassessment of the okapi was conducted, reclassifying it as ‘Endangered’ from ‘Near Threatened’ (Mallon et al., 2013). The giraffe as a species is currently only listed as ‘Least Concern’ on the IUCN Red List. However, two subspecies have been recently classified as ‘Endangered’: the West African giraffe (G. c. peralta; Fennessy & Brown, 2008) and the Rothschild's giraffe (G. c. rothschildi; Fennessy & Brenneman, 2010), and Red List reassessment of the remaining subspecies is underway and planned to be completed in 2015. In this special issue, recent ecological studies are presented, as well as updated information on the conservation status of giraffe and okapi in Africa. The paucity of information highlights the urgent need for additional ecological surveys, population monitoring and conservation of both these emblematic species to ensure their long-term persistence. Regarding this, a number of key issues relate both to the ecological characteristics of each species and to the political context within their range countries. For these individually recognizable species, remotely triggered camera traps can be used to monitor the elusive okapi (Nixon & Lusenge, 2008), which is otherwise hard to directly observe and uses unreliable dung-based survey methods, and photographic surveys can provide useful information on giraffe population size and demography (Suraud et al., 2012). Noninvasive genetic approaches have already demonstrated potential to study the distribution and reproductive behaviour of the okapi (Stanton et al., 2014, 2015) and giraffe (Fennessy et al., 2013; Bock et al., 2014), and could be explored further. Accepting that the popularity and profile of other flagship taxa such as elephant, rhino, big cats and great apes will continue to attract a disproportionate amount of conservation attention and funding, we should also collaborate for example to adapt monitoring of these other taxa to include giraffids as well. The socio-political situation is a major concern in many countries across these species' ranges, necessitating law enforcement on the ground in addition to locally supported, innovative conservation efforts. Given the relative security across much of their respective ranges and the accessibility and visibility of their respective habitats, the potential for tourism-based income and citizen science initiatives is clearly greater for giraffe than okapi. Critically, raising global awareness about the widespread threats to both giraffe and okapi is essential to generate funds and political support for projects on the ground. To this end, the IUCN SSC Giraffe and Okapi Specialist Group was established in March 2013 (www.giraffidsg.org). Its main objective is to increase understanding of giraffe and okapi, the threats they face, and how such threats can be mitigated to facilitate their long-term conservation and to play its part in ensuring the survival of these irreplaceable giraffid cousins.

title: Filling the Humanitarian Gap and a Plural Perspective on Humanitarianism
source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: Communitarian socio-cultural practices ‘from below’ that involve the sharing of material and non-material items play a vital role in the lives of refugees. However, these support practices are rarely discussed, documented, or acknowledged for their contribution to refugees’ protection, livelihoods, and well-being. This article examines communitarian socio-cultural support practices among South Sudanese refugees in Uganda. The article is based on fieldwork conducted between 2021 and 2023 in Bidibidi Refugee Settlement and Uganda’s capital city, Kampala. The objectives of this article are threefold. First, to document the practices that remain invisible in humanitarian discourses but are deemed valuable by refugees to get by in their everyday lives. Second, to examine how communitarian socio-cultural support practices change in contexts of displacement. Third, to discuss the lessons that can be learned from the ethical and philosophical principles informing communitarian socio-cultural support practices in the pursuit of more contextually oriented and inclusive humanitarian practices that recognize, support, and build on the existing capacities of refugees themselves. By documenting the multiple and intricate socio-cultural support practices, we conclude that these practices have the potential to fill gaps in humanitarian practice, such as drawing on resources among refugees to save lives and alleviate suffering, and that the theoretical foundations that inform these practices, such as togetherness, industry, solidarity, hospitality, and ethical and philosophical principles such as responsibility, reciprocity, honesty, humanity, empathy, and so on, can contribute towards expanding the ethical register of humanitarianism. This has the potential to inform debates and discussions on a broadened and more pluralist humanitarian understanding and practice.

title: 137 Building a community of experts in health and migration in the east and horn of Africa region
abstract: Abstract PTH 4: Mental Health and Refugees 2, B307 (FCSH), September 4, 2025, 14:00 - 14:48 Aim Migration and Health has been identified as one of the crosscutting issues in the African Unions’ Migration Policy Framework for Africa. There is high demand to build up a critical mass of expertise and experts on health and migration that can engage in policy, programme and practice development. Methods The Center for Health and Migration, Austria (CHM) in collaboration with the International Organization for Migration (IOM UN-Migration), and the Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, in close cooperation with stakeholders at international, national, and sub-national level, are jointly organizing online courses on Health and Migration. It aims at capacity building in the East and Horn of Africa region in the field of health and migration, building a community of experts who work for and with migrants, refugees, and local communities. The initiative is funded by the Austrian Federal Ministry of the Interior. Results By 2024, 5 courses have been implemented. With the courses, a community of experts has been built up with 332 members from 15 African countries in 2024 in an Alumni database. Participants evaluation shows the importance of the course for capacity building on health and migration in participant’s countries as well as for personal development, and for the improvement of service provision for migrants. For sustainability and further capacity building, the initiative focuses on maintaining network and partnership by engaging alumni and collaborating with regional and national institutions and academia. Conclusions The online course proved to be important for building awareness and competence of professionals in the field of health and migration in the East and Horn of Africa region. Continuous engagement of alumni and networking can support intersectional and interdisciplinary exchange of knowledge and experiences.

title: Exploring barriers and facilitators to HIV+ MSM and TG/Hijra in anti-retroviral treatment (ART) adherence in Mumbai, India
abstract: Background: Though HIV prevalence in refugee settlements in sub-Saharan Africa is usually unknown, the majority of refugees come from neighboring countries where HIV prevalence is high.In Nakivale Refugee Settlement in southwestern Uganda, there are 64,000 refugees from 12 countries.The prevalence of HIV is unknown.We implemented a routine HIV testing program in Nakivale and examined factors associated with new HIV diagnosis.Methods: From Mar-Sept 2013, research assistants routinely offered free HIV-testing to all clients in the Nakivale Clinic Outpatient Department while they waited for their clinic visit.Tested participants were surveyed to obtain demographic information, mode of transport and travel time to clinic.We compared variables for HIV-infected clients and clients not infected with HIV using the Wilcoxon rank sum and Fisher's exact test (continuous, categorical data).We used a logistic regression model to identify predictors of a new diagnosis of HIV-infection among those tested.Findings: Over the 6-month intervention,155 (4.4%) of 3,558 individuals tested were identified with HIV infection.Compared to those without HIV infection, HIV-infected clients had a similar median age (30 vs 29, p¼0.3), were more likely female (68% vs 56%, p¼0.0047), less often refugee (41% vs 71%, p < 0.0001), and had longer median travel time to clinic (90 min vs 60 min, p < 0.0001).Of those tested, males were 0.56 times as likely, those not traveling to clinic on foot were 1.65 times as likely, and those taking longer to reach clinic were 1.07 times (per 15 minutes of travel time) as likely to be found HIV-infected.Likelihood of testing as HIV-infected was significantly associated with country of origin.People from Uganda had the highest prevalence among the individual countries reported, with 93/1,069 (8.7%).Interpretation: In a routine HIV screening program in a refugee settlement in Uganda, Ugandan nationals are at higher risk than most refugees tested.Decentralized testing throughout the refugee settlement may help to identify more individuals with HIV that live further from a health clinic.Given the close physical proximity of refugees and the surrounding Ugandan nationals, future studies should aim to discern if there is HIV transmission and HIV viral mixing among these populations.

title: Transforming lives
abstract: In the first article in a new series focusing on play in emergency settings, Debra Laxton and Sarah Ndlovu outline some of the initiatives the children's rights organisation, Children on the Edge, is facilitating to promote safe play spaces for children in Kyaka Refugee Settlement, Western Uganda.

title: Food Self-Sufficiency
abstract: Abstract This chapter provides a holistic view of Intersectional factors that influence food self-sufficiency through agricultural production among South-Sudanese refugees in Uganda. The chapter points to conflict and instability in the region that contribute to making Uganda a long-term recipient of refugees from neighboring countries. It explains that the nature of asylum in protracted refugee situations has influenced Uganda’s policy to move away from long-term care and maintenance to a durable developmental approach by allocating land to refugee households in designated settlements. The policy assumes that by having access to land, refugees are enabled to produce agricultural output from the land to become food self-sufficient. Using Bronfenbrenner’s ecological model, the chapter analyzes results from a case study in Mungula refugee settlement and describes land security macro-level factors that influence food self-sufficiency at the micro level for South-Sudanese refugee households.

title: Concluding comments to Part II
abstract: This conclusion presents some closing thoughts on the concepts discussed in the preceding chapters of this book. The book presents the experiences of young entrepreneurs living in low-income settlements in Lusaka, Kampala, and Accra reveals how despite living in countries with differing urban characteristics, the types of businesses they establish and the challenges they face are remarkably similar. The urban young entrepreneurs are extremely resourceful in the businesses that they establish, seizing opportunities when they arise and at times turning adversity into opportunity. The young entrepreneurs also feel limited by their lack of education, skills training, and business support services. The insecure and hectic environments in which the young entrepreneurs are working contribute to the insecurity of their businesses. In the case of Nima, the Ghanaian government&s;s slum upgrading programme has resulted in the settlement becoming more attractive to outside investors resulting in some young entrepreneurs being forced out due to rising rents.

title: Mobile payment systems and electronic governance adoption among small and medium enterprises
source: Ndejje University Journal Of Interdisciplinary Studies
abstract: This study focuses on establishing the relationship between mobile payment systems on electronic governance adoption among small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Kampala Central Division. The researcher adopted a cross-sectional design with probabilistic (systematic random sampling) and non-probabilistic (purposive sampling) techniques were used to sample the study participants. A remarkable 94.8% response rate was scored. By virtue of the adjusted R square value (0.191), mobile payment systems contribute only a 19.1% towards a unit change in electronic governance adoption among SMEs in Kampala Central Division. The study affirms that there was adequate evidence to affirm the efficacy of mobile payment systems was a prerequisite for enhancing electronic governance adoption among SMEs not only in Kampala Central Division but also the country at large. It was also affirmed that the digital payment regulatory framework had a remarkable influence on e-governance. UCC should urge mobile providers to integrate interactive tutorials and help features in payment apps, standardizing step-by-step guidance for a consistent user experience across platforms. SMEs should leverage the traceability of transaction card payments for accurate financial tracking and reporting by implementing systems that can quickly retrieve transaction histories for audits and customer inquiries. SMEs should be encouraged to utilize RTGS for transactions that involve substantial sums of money or require immediate settlement.
